start_intro: You are the reactor operator. Keep the plant inside its envelope, follow grid demand and master the faults.
opt_cold_start: Cold start (reactor off, bring it up yourself) -- free play only
reactor_pwr_desc: Two separate loops, 158 bar, no boiling in the core. Power is set with control rods and boric acid. Every feedback is negative — forgiving, but slow to respond.
reactor_bwr_desc: A single loop, steam goes straight to the turbine. Recirculation flow moves power within seconds. At low flow and high power the density-wave instability is waiting.
reactor_rbmk_desc: Graphite moderated, pressure tubes, no full-pressure containment. At low power the void coefficient turns positive. The operating reactivity margin ORM is not a statistic, it is your life insurance.
alarm_help_none: No further explanation on file — the entry already speaks for itself.
stats_cfg_hint: Choose which values appear in the header bar -- separately per reactor type, saved for you. Applies immediately.
glossary_intro: The key terms in short — not a course, just a reference.
shortcuts_intro: Work anywhere during a running game, except while typing in a text field.
sc_escape_d: Close the active help window (alarm help, panel window, briefing)
gl_reactivity_d: How far the core sits from a self-sustaining steady chain reaction. Positive means power is rising on its own. pcm (hundred-thousandths) is the physical unit; $ (dollars) measures the same value relative to the delayed-neutron fraction — at 1 $ the chain reaction goes "prompt critical" (see there).
gl_period_d: Time for power to change by a factor of e (≈2.72). Short and positive means trouble is close. Infinite means stable.
gl_prompt_d: Reactivity reaches the delayed-neutron fraction (β, usually 1 $). From here the chain reaction sustains itself on prompt neutrons alone — power no longer rises over seconds, but over milliseconds.
gl_dnbr_d: Margin to the boiling crisis: how much power is left before the coolant film on the fuel cladding dries out completely and cooling breaks down. DNBR on the pressurized-water design, CPR on the two boiling ones — below 1 the limit is crossed.
gl_subcooling_d: Margin of coolant temperature below the saturation temperature at the current pressure. As it falls toward zero, the coolant starts boiling where the design never intended it to.
gl_xenon_d: Xe-135 builds up during operation and absorbs neutrons. After a power cut it keeps building for hours, fed by the decay of its precursor iodine-135 — reactivity keeps falling before it recovers.
gl_samarium_d: Sm-149 acts like xenon but is stable — it doesn't decay away, it has to be burned out by fissioning. After a long shutdown the poisoning just sits there instead of fading.
gl_orm_d: On the RBMK: how many control rods, in rod-equivalents, are still in the core. Not just a readout — it's the parameter that sets the void coefficient. The emptier the core, the more positive its response to boiling.
gl_void_d: How reactivity responds to steam voids in the coolant. Negative (pressurized- and boiling-water designs) is self-limiting: more steam means less reactivity. Positive (RBMK at low operating margin) is self-reinforcing.
gl_doppler_d: As fuel temperature rises, the U-238 resonances broaden and absorb more neutrons — always negative, acts instantly, and the fastest built-in brake on all three plant types.
gl_decay_d: Heat from the radioactive decay of fission products, which keeps going even after a scram — starting around 7% of rated power, then fading slowly over hours and days. The reason a shut-down core still needs cooling.
gl_scram_d: Reactor trip: every rod drives in at maximum speed. Named differently by control room — RESA in German, SCRAM in American usage, AZ-5 on the RBMK. Never fires on its own — what a given alarm means is in its own help text on the annunciator.
gl_annun_d: New (fast blink + horn): just came in, unacknowledged. Acknowledged (steady light): seen, cause still present. Cleared (slow blink): cause gone, but not yet acknowledged. Dark: everything normal.
empty_stage: This area is filled in a later version.
fault_body: The simulation reached an invalid state and was stopped. That is a bug in the game, not your mistake.
footer_note: Physically modelled, but a game — not a training simulator.
reactor_soon_hint: This type arrives in a later version. The pressurised water reactor is already playable.
ctl_boron_hint: Takes about three minutes to arrive.
trip_power_high_help:
Neutron flux above the permitted limit — 112 % on the PWR and RBMK, 118 % on the BWR. The chain reaction is sustaining itself; without action power keeps climbing within seconds.

Do this now:
1. Scram immediately — button at the top right of the header (SCRAM, AZ-5 on the RBMK), press twice. Nothing else acts fast enough.
2. Then find the cause before restarting. Usually it is withdrawing "Control rods" too fast (Reactor core panel) or too large a step on "Load demand" (Generator and grid panel).
3. To restart, first press "Reset" on the annunciator. That only works once no trip condition is standing any more — a protection system that clears itself during the fault would not be one.
trip_period_short_help:
Reactor period below 10 seconds with the chain reaction running: power doubles every few seconds. That runs away faster than any controller can follow.

Do this now:
1. Scram immediately (SCRAM/AZ-5, header, press twice).
2. The cause is almost always withdrawing "Control rods" too fast (Reactor core panel) or an unintended reactivity addition — on the PWR "Boric acid → Dilute" (Reactor chemistry panel).
3. Afterwards move the rods far more slowly, or leave "Rod control" / "Power controller" (Reactor core panel) in automatic.

For scale: a 10 s period means a factor of e every 10 seconds, so roughly twentyfold in one minute.
trip_pzr_press_low_help:
Pressurizer pressure below 132 bar. Usually a leak — a stuck relief valve, say — or too much spray with too little heating.

Why this is dangerous: as pressure falls so does the coolant’s boiling temperature, and with it the subcooling margin. Once that reaches zero the core is no longer in water but in steam — and steam absorbs heat instead of carrying it away.

Do this now:
1. If the annunciator also shows "Relief valve stuck open", first set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary loop panel). That stops the leak; everything else is futile until it is shut.
2. Scram.
3. Check "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary loop panel). If it is in automatic and that is not enough, switch to manual and raise it.
4. Back off "Pressuriser spray" if it is open in manual.

The indication that matters is the subcooling margin, not pressure itself.
trip_pzr_press_high_help:
Pressurizer pressure above 166 bar — usually too little spray while power is rising. The relief valve opens by design at 162 bar, the safety valves at 171 bar.

Do this now:
1. Scram.
2. Switch "Pressuriser spray" (Secondary loop panel) to manual and open it if automatic cannot keep up.
3. Back off "Pressuriser heaters". Never run both at once — alternating heating and spraying is the fastest way to wreck a pressurizer.
4. Afterwards change power more slowly; fast ramps are the usual cause.
trip_pzr_level_low_help:
Pressurizer level below 17 %. Not yet a trip, but the precursor to a pressure drop: the pressurizer is the primary circuit’s steam cushion, and an empty one cannot hold pressure.

Do this now:
• Check whether a leak is behind it: does the annunciator show "Relief valve open" or "Relief valve stuck open"? Then that is the cause — set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary loop panel).
• Slow the power ramp until level recovers. Level follows average coolant temperature: as the primary cools, the water contracts and the pressurizer drains.
• If level does not come back, prepare for a real pressure excursion (see "Pressure low").
trip_dnbr_low_help:
DNBR below 1.3 — the margin to departure from nucleate boiling at the cladding is nearly used up. Below 1.0 the water film breaks down and the cladding overheats locally within seconds.

Three quantities set the DNBR: more flow helps, more power hurts, less subcooling hurts.

Do this now:
1. Scram. The DNBR will not recover on its own while power and flow stand as they are.
2. Check "Reactor coolant pumps" (Primary loop panel) — is every one running? A tripped pump can be clicked there and restarted.
3. If "Subcooling low" is standing as well, low pressure is the real cause rather than power — see that entry instead.
4. After resetting, start up more slowly and only take power back once all pumps are running.
trip_sg_level_low_help:
Steam generator level below 25 %. The tube bundles risk uncovering, and the feedwater pumps risk cavitation. The steam generator is the primary circuit’s heat sink — lose it and the core has nowhere to send its heat.

Do this now:
1. Scram.
2. Check "Feedwater" (Secondary loop panel): if it is in automatic and level still falls, switch to manual and raise it.
3. The cause is usually a feedwater failure or too much steam being drawn — "Governor valve" (Secondary loop panel) open too far.

Careful reading it: after a load rejection pressure falls, the water swells, and the indication rises briefly even though water is missing.
alarm_sg_level_high_help:
Steam generator level above 78 % — risk of water being carried over with the steam to the turbine (water hammer).

Do this now:
• Throttle "Feedwater" (Secondary loop panel), switching briefly to manual and lowering the value if needed.
• Check whether a load step simply made the controller overshoot — then waiting is enough. The feedwater controller uses steam flow as feedforward and needs a few seconds to settle.
alarm_sg_press_high_help:
Steam generator pressure above 84 bar: the governor valve is not taking enough steam. Usually power is rising faster than the turbine follows. At 88 bar the secondary safety valves lift.

Do this now:
• Check "Governor valve" (Secondary loop panel): if it is in automatic, switch briefly to manual and open it further.
• Or back off "Load demand" (Generator and grid panel) until pressure settles.
• The steam dump catches the excess by itself above 72 bar and routes it past the turbine to the condenser. It needs no operator action, but its contribution is shown on the Secondary loop panel.
trip_rcp_lost_help:
Coolant flow below 60 % of nominal. At least one reactor coolant pump has tripped or been switched off, and the rest cannot carry the cooling alone.

There is a second possible cause, and it is the more dangerous one: the pumps are running but moving steam instead of water. A centrifugal pump moves volume — if the coolant flashes as pressure falls, mass flow collapses even though nothing about the speed has changed.

Do this now:
1. Scram.
2. Check "Reactor coolant pumps" (Primary loop panel). A tripped pump can be clicked there and restarted.
3. If the subcooling margin is at or below zero, the pump is not the problem — pressure is. Stop the leak first ("Block valve", Primary loop panel) and rebuild pressure.
4. Only take power back after resetting and with every pump running.
alarm_subcool_low_help:
Subcooling margin below 8 K. The coolant is approaching the boiling temperature that belongs to the pressure currently present.

This is the primary circuit’s most important indication. It says how far the water in the core still is from boiling. Once it reaches zero the core is no longer in water but in steam — steam absorbs heat but does not carry it away, and from then on you have minutes.

Do this now:
1. Find out why pressure is falling. If "Relief valve stuck open" is standing, set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary loop panel) — that is both the cause and the cure.
2. Raise pressure: switch "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary loop panel) to manual and turn them up, close "Pressuriser spray".
3. Alternatively or additionally lower power before the DNBR limit is reached.
4. Check "Reactor coolant pumps" — less flow makes it worse still.
alarm_porv_open_help:
The pressurizer relief valve is open and relieving pressure. It opens by design at 162 bar and re-closes on its own as pressure falls.

The dangerous case is the other one: if the message stays up although pressure is long back below the setpoint, the valve is stuck. The separate message "Relief valve stuck open" then appears too — and waiting for it to snap shut is futile, because coolant is being lost continuously.

Do this now:
• If the message comes after a pressure peak and clears again: nothing further is needed, high pressure was the cause. Check "Pressuriser spray" and "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary loop panel) so it does not recur.
• If it stays up: set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary loop panel). It sits in series ahead of the relief valve and isolates it.
• Read pressurizer level and subcooling margin alongside — they show first whether coolant is genuinely being lost.
alarm_turbine_trip_help:
The turbine has tripped: the generator is off the grid and no load is being taken. The reactor’s heat now has to go through the steam dump to the condenser, and whatever is left through the safety valves.

Do this now:
1. Stabilise the plant: watch pressure and level, both swing hard after a load rejection.
2. Only once things are quiet, reconnect via "Reconnect turbine" (Generator and grid panel). The button only works if no scram is standing — coupling a turbine to a reactor that has just been shut down has no purpose and no steam behind it.
3. Then raise "Load demand" (same panel) slowly.

If the trip came together with a scram, the annunciator has to be reset first.
trip_clad_temp_help:
Cladding temperature above 1204 °C. Beyond this point the zirconium-water reaction sustains itself, generating its own heat and hydrogen with it. If it stays there for more than three minutes the core is lost — with no power excursion at all, purely from lost cooling.

Do this now:
1. Scram immediately if you have not already.
2. Restore cooling. That is the real task, and which route is left depends on what still works:
   – "Reactor coolant pumps" or "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel), if power and water are available;
   – "Isolation condenser" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section), if main steam is isolated;
   – "Fire-main injection" (same section), if there is no power at all — it needs no motor and no electronics.
3. Check pressure: if the subcooling margin is below zero the core is dry and more pump speed achieves nothing. Rebuild pressure first.
event_h2_explosion: Hydrogen explosion in the reactor building
event_time_skip: Time skipped ahead until the xenon had decayed
trip_dome_press_high_help:
Dome or drum pressure above the permitted value (78.5 bar on the BWR, 76 bar on the RBMK). Less steam is leaving than the core is producing.

On the BWR this is particularly awkward: rising pressure collapses the steam voids in the core, fewer voids mean more moderator, and more moderator means MORE power. The pressure rise drives itself.

First work out WHY the steam cannot get away:

Is "Main steam isolated" or "Main steam isolation stuck" also standing?
Then the governor valve and steam dump are useless — they sit DOWNSTREAM of the isolation valves and no steam reaches them. Opening them changes nothing. Instead:
1. Scram (header, press twice).
2. Set "Isolation condenser" to "open" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section). It is now the only heat sink and only works with the reactor shut down — hence step 1 first.
3. Watch containment pressure and vent in good time.

Isolation not standing?
Then the path is clear and the valves genuinely help:
• Switch "Governor valve" (Secondary loop panel) to manual and open further.
• The steam dump opens by itself 4 bar above operating pressure.
• On the BWR, back off "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel) — that lowers power directly without moving a single rod.

Above 78 bar the safety valves blow into the suppression pool. That saves the vessel but fills the containment.
trip_level_low_help:
Level below 25 % — core coverage is at risk. Once fuel is uncovered only passing steam cools it, and heat transfer collapses to a fraction.

Do this now:
1. Scram.
2. Check "Feedwater" (Secondary loop panel): if automatic is not enough, switch to manual and raise it.
3. With no AC power the feedwater pumps and their control are dead. Then only "Fire-main injection" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section) is left — it needs no motor and no electronics, but delivers far less.
4. Only take power back once level is stable in the normal band.

Do not trust the indication blindly: the measurement needs DC power. Without it the reading freezes at its last value while the vessel keeps draining. That is exactly what misled the control room at Fukushima in 2011.
alarm_level_high_help:
Level above 78 % — risk of water being carried over with the steam to the turbine.

Do this now:
• Throttle "Feedwater" (Secondary loop panel), switching to manual and lowering it if needed.
• Check whether a load change simply made the controller overshoot — then waiting is enough.
• If level keeps rising despite reduced feed, less steam is leaving than is being made: check the steam path (see "Dome pressure high").
trip_oprm_help:
Power oscillation detected, the OPRM limit has been exceeded. The operating point is stuck in the excluded corner of the power-flow map: high power, too little recirculation flow.

What happens there: steam quality, pressure drop and flow couple into a density wave that grows instead of decaying. It keeps growing on its own until cladding damage becomes likely.

Do this now:
1. Scram. With an OPRM message standing this is the only safe route — the oscillation grows faster than the operating point can be moved.
2. The cause was "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel) too low for the power being run.
3. In future: raise flow FIRST, then bring power up with the rods. The other order routes you straight through the excluded corner.
alarm_instability_help:
Signs of a power oscillation: the decay ratio is approaching 1. At 1 a disturbance no longer decays at all; above it, it grows. Not yet an OPRM trip, but the precursor — and right now it can still be fixed without a shutdown.

Do this now:
1. Raise "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel). More flow sweeps the voids out and damps the oscillation directly — the fastest and most effective lever.
2. If that is not enough, lower power until the operating point leaves the excluded corner: "Control rods → Insert" (Reactor core panel).

Do not ignore both. Without action the oscillation grows until the OPRM trips, and then only a scram is left.
alarm_recirc_low_help:
Recirculation flow low at high power. This operating point sits at the edge of the instability region — the early warning before the density-wave oscillation.

Do this now:
1. Raise "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel) BEFORE power rises further.
2. If that is not enough, lower power rather than holding it with the rods.

Rule of thumb for this plant type: flow first, power second. Take power first and you drive through the excluded corner of the map.
alarm_msiv_closed_help:
The main steam isolation valves are shut. No steam reaches the turbine and none reaches the condenser — the core’s heat has nowhere to go, and reactor pressure is rising.

Important: "Governor valve" and the steam dump do NOT help here. Both sit downstream of the isolation valves, so no steam reaches them. Opening them changes nothing.

Do this now, in this order:
1. Scram (header, press twice). With no steam path there is no heat sink; the core has to come down, or rising pressure will drive power up as well through void collapse.
2. Set "Isolation condenser" to "open" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section). It is now the only heat sink. It only works if the reactor is scrammed AND main steam is isolated AND its supply lasts — hence step 1 first, or nothing happens.
3. Watch containment pressure: the safety valves blow into the suppression pool above 78 bar and it fills up. Above 3.5 bar open "Containment vent" (same section).

If "Main steam isolation stuck" is standing as well, the valves cannot be reopened at all — then the order above is not merely the fastest route but the only one.
alarm_srv_open_help:
A safety valve has lifted. Above 78 bar dome pressure it opens by itself and closes again by itself as pressure falls — there is nothing to do at the valve.

The cost is the real point: that steam does not go to the condenser but into the suppression pool inside containment, which fills up and has nowhere to discharge. Every minute of blowdown spends containment margin.

Do this now — fix the cause, not the valve:
• Is "Main steam isolated" standing? Then the steam path is shut and only a scram plus the isolation condenser helps (see that entry).
• Otherwise: open "Governor valve" (Secondary loop panel) further, or lower power — on the BWR via "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel).
• Read containment pressure alongside.
alarm_cont_press_high_help:
Containment pressure above 3.5 bar. The safety valves are blowing steam into the suppression pool and the containment has nowhere to discharge. Above 4.3 bar it fails — and the run ends there, even if the core is still intact at that moment.

Do this now:
1. Set "Containment vent" to "open" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section) BEFORE design pressure is reached. A controlled release beats an uncontrolled break.
2. Address the cause so the safety valves stop lifting: that means power down and a heat sink restored (see "Dome pressure high").

For scale: venting cannot win against a reactor still at power — the inflow is many times larger. It can win against the decay heat of a shut-down reactor. That is why the order is scram first, vent second, and not the other way round.

If a lot of hydrogen is present as well, vent as early as possible — the longer you wait the more accumulates.
alarm_h2_critical_help:
Hydrogen from the zirconium-water reaction inside containment. The cladding is already damaged: the reaction starts above 1200 °C cladding temperature, long before the fuel itself melts.

Do this now:
1. Vent immediately (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section) before more accumulates. Hydrogen that finds its own way out late and in quantity can explode inside the reactor building — exactly what happened at Fukushima Daiichi in 2011.
2. Lower cladding temperature wherever possible: check "Isolation condenser", otherwise "Fire-main injection" (same section). While the cladding stays above 1200 °C the hydrogen inventory keeps growing.

This message does not clear once the cladding is damaged. From here on the only thing that counts is not losing the core as well.
alarm_orm_low_help:
Operating reactivity margin (ORM) below 30 rod equivalents. Outside the permitted band per operating rules, even though nothing has tripped yet.

Why this is more than a rule on the RBMK: the further the rods are out, the more positive the void coefficient becomes. The core then amplifies its own disturbances instead of damping them — while less and less margin remains to stop it.

Do this now:
1. "Control rods → Insert" (Reactor core panel) rather than withdrawing further.
2. Do not raise power until the ORM is back above 30.
3. If "Power controller" is in automatic and withdrawing rods by itself (because xenon is building), that is the cause — lower the power setpoint instead of fighting it.
alarm_orm_critical_help:
Operating reactivity margin below 15. This is the most dangerous state this plant type has.

With the rods this far out, AZ-5 inserts POSITIVE reactivity for the first few seconds instead of negative: the graphite tips on the rod ends displace water from the lower core first, and graphite moderates better than water. The shutdown raises power before it lowers it. That is exactly how Chernobyl unfolded in 1986.

Do this now:
1. "Control rods → Insert" (Reactor core panel) immediately, by hand, while there is still margin to do it.
2. Lower power: backing off "Main circulation pumps" (Primary loop panel) acts more slowly than the rods here, but it helps.
3. Pressing AZ-5 now is risky and is the last resort, only when nothing else remains. See also the glossary under "SCRAM / RESA / AZ-5".
alarm_void_positive_help:
The void coefficient has gone strongly positive. More steam voids in the coolant now mean MORE reactivity, not less — the core amplifies its own disturbances.

The cause is almost always too little shutdown margin: the further the rods are out, the more positive the coefficient.

Do this now:
1. "Control rods → Insert" (Reactor core panel) — raising the margin defuses the coefficient directly. This is the most effective lever.
2. Keep "Main circulation pumps" (Primary loop panel) up: enough flow keeps the void fraction in the core small, so there is less for the coefficient to amplify.
3. Do not run in the low power range — the effect is strongest there and the plant is hardest to hold.
alarm_mcp_cavitation_help:
Subcooling below 4 K at more than 90 % of nominal flow: the pumps are running too fast for water this hot and this close to boiling. Voids form on the suction side and collapse violently further in — that eats impellers and makes delivery collapse.

Do this now:
1. Back off "Main circulation pumps" (Primary loop panel). Less flow lowers the suction draw and defuses the cavitation directly.
2. Check drum pressure — it should sit near 69 bar. Too low means saturation temperature falls, the water is closer to boiling, and subcooling shrinks.
3. Check drum level: too little feedwater lets hotter, steam-laden water return to the pumps instead of cool water.

Careful with step 1: on the RBMK less flow also means more voids in the core and therefore positive reactivity. Back off slowly and keep an eye on power.
alarm_graphite_hot_help:
Graphite temperature above 760 °C — the moderator is overheating. Because of its long time constant of about 35 minutes this value responds late, and it decays just as slowly.

Do this now:
• Lower power and HOLD it there. Corrective action here takes minutes to hours to show, not seconds — coming back up after two minutes because nothing visible happened achieves nothing.
• Not a reason to scram on its own, but a reliable sign that the plant has been run too high for too long.
alarm_axial_tilt_help:
Axial power tilt above 35 %: the upper or lower core carries markedly more power than the rest. The cause is usually a xenon oscillation rather than rod position — xenon burns out where flux is high, so power rises further exactly there while the other half of the core poisons.

Do this now:
• Do not raise power further until the profile evens out. Depending on the xenon state that takes hours — the oscillation has a period of roughly half a day.
• Check "Control rods" (Reactor core panel), but expect little: on the RBMK both banks move together, which is a poor tool against a xenon distribution.
• See the glossary under "Xenon poisoning (iodine pit)".
az5_hint: AZ-5 drives every rod in over 18 seconds — graphite tips first.
scn_free_desc: No orders, no score. The plant is yours.
scn_pwr_load_follow_brief:
Day shift at the pressurized-water plant. At midday the grid pulls its load back — heavy industry easing off together — and your unit is to follow it down, then climb back up through the afternoon, staying inside the demand curve throughout. Normally the control rods handle load changes like this: small, barely noticeable moves. But somewhere in this shift a rod bank jams, likely a drive fault, and there's no time to fix it mid-run. From then on boron is the only lever left for reactivity — and boron is slow: a good three minutes before a concentration change even reaches the core. Fail to plan for that lag, and you fall behind the curve.

What matters here:
• Follow the demand curve — while the rods obey, "Rod control" (Reactor core panel) in automatic does it for you.
• Once the bank jams, "Boric acid" (Reactor chemistry panel) is all that is left: diluting raises power, borating lowers it.
• Because of the three-minute dead time, dose EARLY and in small steps, then "Stop" — wait until the deviation is visible and you will always be dosing behind the curve and overshooting.
scn_pwr_turbine_trip_brief:
Full-power shift at the pressurized-water plant — until, ten minutes in, the turbine trips without warning. The generator drops off the grid instantly, but the reactor keeps making the same heat it always did: it now has to go straight to the condenser through the steam dump system, while the pressurizer and steam generator level swing out of balance. Just as you get that under control, feedwater regulation fails too — from there you're chasing level by hand while pressure tries to settle. Two faults that would each be manageable alone, arriving back to back.

What matters here:
• After the trip the steam dump takes the steam by itself, above 72 bar. It needs no operator action — watch the pressurizer and steam generator level instead.
• When feedwater regulation fails: switch "Feedwater" (Secondary loop panel) to manual and hold level yourself, setpoint 50 %.
• Only once things are steady, "Reconnect turbine" (Generator and grid panel), then raise "Load demand" slowly.
scn_bwr_flow_brief:
Three hours of load following at the boiling-water plant, this time driven through recirculation flow rather than the rods — the usual method here for smaller, fast load changes. The grid wants less at midday and more again in the afternoon; you follow by steering throughput across the power/flow map. The excluded corner sits where high power meets low flow — the decay ratio of the power oscillation that forms there grows instead of dying out. Partway through, the recirculation pump runs back on its own, unrequested: flow drops, and that forbidden corner gets closer whether you asked for it or not.

What matters here:
• "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel) is the power control on this plant — more flow sweeps voids out and raises power within seconds, without touching a rod.
• Rule of thumb: flow first, power second. The other order routes you through the excluded corner of the map.
• When "Recirculation low" appears that is the early warning — raise flow at once rather than holding power with the rods.
scn_bwr_msiv_brief:
Full power at the boiling-water plant, a quiet first few minutes — then, seven minutes in, the main steam isolation valves shut without warning. The steam path to the condenser is gone, pressure in the reactor vessel spikes, and as pressure climbs the voids in the core collapse. Fewer voids means more moderation, means positive reactivity — arriving exactly when there is the least time to spare. You have seconds, not minutes, to respond.

What matters here:
• "Governor valve" and the steam dump do NOT help — they sit downstream of the isolation valves and no steam reaches them.
1. Scram (header, press twice).
2. Set "Isolation condenser" to "open" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section). It only works with the reactor shut down — hence step 1 first.
3. Watch containment pressure; above 3.5 bar open "Containment vent".
scn_rbmk_night_brief:
Night shift on the RBMK, in the middle of a planned grid test: power is to come down from 1000 to 200 megawatts, hold there for a while, then climb back up — on paper, a routine exercise. But 200 megawatts is exactly where this reactor type turns dangerous. Xenon builds up and eats into reactivity, forcing the control rods further out to compensate — and that eats into the operating reactivity margin, the number of rod-equivalents that must stay available in the core for an emergency. Below 30 rods, operation is already against the rules. Below 15, the AZ-5 scram stops being a safety function and becomes its opposite: the graphite tips that insert first displace what little moderation is left where the water has already boiled away, igniting reactivity instead of killing it. The power regulator drops out mid-shift, and shortly after, two main circulation pumps trip — both have to be caught by hand while the shutdown margin keeps shrinking.

What matters here:
• The operating reactivity margin (ORM) is the number everything comes down to. Below 30 you are outside the rules; below 15, AZ-5 raises power first instead of lowering it.
• If "Power controller" (Reactor core panel) fails, hold power yourself with "Control rods → Withdraw/Insert".
• If pumps trip: "Main circulation pumps" (Primary loop panel) — less flow means more voids here and therefore POSITIVE reactivity, so move slowly and watch power.
• When in doubt lower power and insert rods. Winning margin back matters more than the demand curve.
scn_pwr_porv_brief:
A quiet full-power shift at the pressurized-water plant — until, sometime in the first quarter hour, the pressurizer relief valve opens as designed to bleed off a small pressure rise, and then sticks: it stays open, while the control board still reports it shut. Pressure and level in the pressurizer fall as coolant quietly bleeds away through the open valve. The annunciator warns early, if you're watching for it — trust the position indication over the alarm, and you lose subcooling margin first, then the margin to boiling at the fuel surface (DNBR). The exact failure that started the Three Mile Island accident in 1979 — there, because no one trusted the contradiction between the two readings.

What matters here:
• The indication that counts is the subcooling margin — not pressurizer level. Once it falls below zero the core is in steam, not water.
1. Set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary loop panel). The only action that stops the leak, and it works immediately.
2. Scram.
3. Switch "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary loop panel) to manual and raise them, close "Pressuriser spray", until pressure holds again.
• At Three Mile Island, step 1 took two and a half hours.
scn_bwr_fukushima_brief:
Five minutes into the shift, the earthquake: automatic scram and isolation, the isolation condenser takes over decay-heat removal exactly as designed — no power needed for its core function. Fifty minutes later, the tsunami: total loss of power, AC and DC both gone at once. The isolation condenser fails to its safe default position — SHUT — and stays there, unnoticed, because its own indicator needs the very power that just disappeared and keeps showing its last known state. From here on, only what needs no electricity at all still works — valves opened by hand, gravity, and the decay heat still sitting in the core with nowhere else to go.

What matters here:
• Without DC power the level indication lies: it freezes at its last value while the vessel keeps draining. Do not trust it.
• "Isolation condenser" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section) needs DC power for its valves — without it the valve falls shut whatever the indication says.
• Without AC power only "Fire-main injection" (same section) is left: no motor, no electronics, but far less flow.
• Open "Containment vent" early rather than late — the longer you wait the more hydrogen accumulates.
scn_bwr_instab_brief:
Full-power shift at the boiling-water plant, grid demand staying high — then the main recirculation pumps drop back to low flow on their own, nothing you asked for. Power doesn't follow immediately, tempting you to chase it with the control rods instead of restoring flow first. That's exactly what drives the core into the excluded corner of the power/flow map: high power, low flow. There, a density-wave oscillation grows by itself, with no further cause needed, until the OPRM power limiter trips — and the scram doesn't fire on its own; you have to trigger it yourself when it's time.

What matters here:
• Raising "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel) is the countermeasure: more flow damps the density wave directly.
• When "Instability" appears there is still time for that. When "Oscillation" (OPRM) appears there is not — then only a scram is left.
• The annunciator shuts nothing down. The button at the top right is yours.
scn_rbmk_cold_brief:
Early shift after a two-week outage: the unit stands completely cold, every control rod fully inserted, the main circulation pumps stopped. Your job: bring the plant from shutdown onto the grid. First start the circulation pumps and establish flow, then ease the rods out until the core goes critical and power starts to climb. On an RBMK, that climb is the most dangerous part of the shift: the fuel is still cold, so the Doppler effect — the strongest natural brake against rising power — is weak, and the positive void coefficient carries more weight than it would at full power. You have to pass through the same 200-megawatt zone the night shift warns about, only this time climbing up into it instead of sitting in it — starting with the shutdown margin nearly full, but every centimeter of rod withdrawn spends down the very margin you'd need in a real fault. Target: 900 megawatts, without ever letting that margin fall below 30 rod-equivalents — and without ever seeing 15.

What matters here:
• A cold start means all rods in and the core subcritical. Bring it up with "Control rods → Withdraw" (Reactor core panel), in small steps.
• Keep an eye on the period. Below 10 seconds the trip message appears — a period of 20 to 40 seconds is brisk enough.
• Start the pumps before the power arrives: "Main circulation pumps" (Primary loop panel).
• Read the shutdown margin alongside. The target is 900 MW without dropping below 30 rod equivalents.

alarm_rod_stuck_help:
A control rod bank no longer follows its demand — the drive is jammed. The demand can still be changed, the position will not follow, and a scram will not drive this bank in either.

Do this now:
• Stop commanding that rod. It will not move, and the demand drifts further from the real position with every click — after that you no longer know where you stand.
• Control reactivity by this plant’s other route:
   – PWR: "Boric acid" (Reactor chemistry panel). Borating lowers power, diluting raises it — both with about three minutes of delay, so dose early and in small steps.
   – BWR: "Recirculation flow" (Primary loop panel). More flow sweeps voids out and raises power, less lowers it — in seconds rather than minutes.
   – RBMK: the remaining rod banks.
• Watch the shutdown margin: a jammed bank is missing from any scram, and the remaining banks have to do it alone.
alarm_msiv_stuck_help:
The main steam isolation valves are shut and can NO LONGER be opened — the actuator does not respond. Setting "Main steam isolation" to "open" does nothing: the position snaps straight back. The steam path to the turbine and condenser is permanently closed, so the core’s heat has nowhere to go.

Equally useless: "Governor valve" and the steam dump. Both sit downstream of the isolation valves, so no steam reaches them.

Do this now, in this order:
1. Scram (header, press twice). With no steam path there is no heat sink — otherwise dome pressure runs away, the safety valves blow into the suppression pool, and the containment fills up.
2. Set "Isolation condenser" to "open" (Secondary loop panel, Safety systems section). It is now the only heat sink. It only works if the reactor is scrammed AND main steam is isolated AND its supply lasts — hence step 1 first, or nothing happens.
3. Watch containment pressure. Above 3.5 bar open "Containment vent" (same section) before it reaches 4.3 bar.
alarm_porv_stuck_help:
The pressurizer relief valve has stayed open even though pressure is long back below its setpoint. It will NOT re-close on its own — waiting for that indication is futile. While it stands open the primary circuit loses coolant continuously: pressure and pressurizer level fall, and once pressure drops below the boiling point of the hot coolant, the core flashes to steam and runs dry.

This is exactly the Three Mile Island failure of 1979. There it took two and a half hours before anyone realised a valve was open.

Do this now, in this order:
1. Set "Block valve" to "shut" (Primary loop panel). It sits in series ahead of the relief valve and isolates it — the only action that stops the leak, and it works immediately.
2. Scram, if you have not already.
3. Switch "Pressuriser heaters" (Secondary loop panel) to manual and raise them, close "Pressuriser spray", until pressure holds again.

The indication that matters is the subcooling margin. Once it falls below zero the core is no longer in water but in steam. From then on you have minutes.
event_fuel_dispersal_body: Fuel enthalpy exceeded 963 J/g. The fuel has dispersed and the plant is lost. This is how a fast power excursion ends: more reactivity than the feedbacks could remove in the time available.
event_clad_failure_body: Cladding temperature stayed above 1204 °C for more than three minutes. Beyond that point the zirconium-water reaction sustains itself, generating its own heat and hydrogen with it. The core is lost — with no power excursion at all, purely from lost cooling.
event_coolant_loss_body: Subcooling stayed below zero for more than five minutes: the core was no longer sitting in water but in steam. Steam absorbs heat, it does not carry it away. From the moment subcooling goes negative you have minutes — that was the indication that mattered.
event_cont_failure_loss_body: Containment exceeded its design pressure of 4.3 bar and ruptured. The last barrier between fission products and the environment is gone. Venting in time would have relieved the pressure — a controlled release instead of an uncontrolled break.
